rationale: With every finding and correction recorded, this turn chased one more suspicion of the same family as the log-read paths that replication and commit decisions depend on: that the log cache could serve an entry that the log store no longer agrees with, because the cache keeps the caller's pointers and a producer that mutates a Log after storing it would leave the two views different. The answer is a scoped negative and it is worth recording as one. The cache validates each ring slot by index equality and falls through to the store on any mismatch, clears the ring before deleting in the store, and stores exactly the pointers it was handed; the in-memory store keeps the same pointers, so cache and store share the objects and cannot disagree on an entry's value. On the producer side no non-test call site mutates a Log after handing it to the store: the leader fills index, term and timestamp before storing, the follower stores the decoded entries and only reads them afterwards, and bootstrap writes one entry and returns. The hazard therefore exists only for an external caller that mutates a Log after storing it while using a store that copies on write, such as a disk store that serializes, where the cache would then serve the mutated object while the durable copy kept the original. I record that boundary rather than inflating it into a defect, and I record the suspicion as refuted for in-tree producers with the reason stated.

investigations.question: Can the log cache serve an entry value that the underlying log store no longer agrees with, for producers inside this package?
investigations.hypothesis: The cache keeps the caller's Log pointers in its ring and returns a cached entry when the slot's index matches, so its view agrees with the store only as long as nothing mutates a stored Log afterwards, or as long as the store keeps the same object rather than a copy. The in-memory store keeps the same pointers, so for that store the two views are the same objects; for a copying store, a caller that mutates a stored Log would make the cache serve the mutated value while the durable copy kept the original.
investigations.discriminator: Check every non-test producer that hands a Log to the store: if each finishes filling an entry before storing it and never mutates it afterwards, then no in-tree producer can make the cache and the store disagree, and the residual hazard is confined to external callers using a copying store. Reading settles it, so no execution is spent.

knowledge.statement: LogCache.GetLog validates a ring slot by comparing the cached entry's index with the requested one and otherwise falls through to the store, DeleteRange clears the whole ring before the store deletes, and StoreLogs caches exactly the pointers it was given; the in-memory store keeps the same pointers, so for that store the cache and the store hold the same objects. Every non-test producer fills the entry (index, term, timestamp) before storing it and only reads it afterwards - the leader in dispatchLogs, the follower in appendEntries, and BootstrapCluster which writes one entry and returns.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, producers inside the package, with the in-memory store or any store that keeps the pointers it is given. The agreement claim does not extend to an external caller that mutates a Log after storing it while the store copies on write.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion was that the cache could serve an entry value the store no longer agrees with, which would matter because replication and commit decisions read through the log store. Reading refutes it for in-tree producers on two independent grounds. First, the cache's read path is conservative: it returns a cached entry only when the ring slot's index matches the requested index, and otherwise asks the store, so a mis-keyed slot is a miss rather than a wrong answer, and a delete clears the whole ring before the store deletes, so a truncated suffix cannot be served from the cache. Second, the two views hold the same objects: StoreLogs caches the pointers it was handed and the in-memory store keeps those same pointers, so a mutation would move both views together rather than separating them. On the producer side, each non-test call site fills the entry before storing it and never mutates it afterwards - the leader assigns index, term and timestamp in the loop before StoreLogs, the follower stores the entries decoded from the request and then only reads them, and bootstrap writes a single entry and returns. The residual hazard is therefore real but external and narrower than the suspicion: a caller that hands a Log to a copying store - a disk store that serializes - and then mutates that same Log would have the cache serving the mutated object while the durable copy keeps the original, because the cache keeps the caller's pointer while the store kept bytes. That is a boundary worth stating for callers, not a defect of the in-tree producers, and I record it as such rather than dressing it up.
counterevidence: The refutation is scoped to in-tree producers and to stores that keep the pointers they are given; with a serializing store plus an external caller that mutates a stored Log, the two views can differ, which is the case the boundary names.

This is a source-level negative with no execution behind it, which is appropriate for a claim about which code paths mutate what, but it does not measure what any particular external store implementation keeps.

The cache's conservative read path means a divergence would show up as a stale-but-index-matching entry rather than a wrong index, so the observable effect of the external hazard would be subtler than a mismatch in keys.
limitations: No execution: the negative rests on reading the cache, the in-memory store and the three producers, not on a test that mutates a stored entry.
Only the in-package producers were checked; an application that wraps its own store and reuses Log values remains the case the boundary describes.
